687.title: Greater than our heart (1 John 3:19–24)
687.hook: when our heart condemns us, God is greater than our heart
687.howItsDone: Pastors and spiritual directors often turn to 1 John 3:20 with people troubled by guilt or a harsh conscience, and many Christians memorize it as a comfort.

segments.voice: Yesterday, in deed and in truth, and your line was not in word only. Which small deed did you do before saying anything about it? Day six hundred eighty-seven.

Some people have a prosecutor living in their head. You know the voice. It replays the awkward thing you said at the party. It reminds you of the mistake from ten years ago. It says, you call that love? After yesterday's passage, about loving in deed and in truth, that voice might be loud. Did I do enough? Have I ever really loved anyone that way? The writer of First John seems to know that his own words can set off the prosecutor. So right after asking for real, costly love, he turns to the reader whose heart is condemning them.

He says that by loving in deed we come to know we are of the truth, and "shall assure our hearts before him." Assure, here, means to calm, to persuade, to quiet down. Then the line: "For if our heart condemn us, God is greater than our heart, and knoweth all things." Christians have heard this in two ways, and it's honest to say so. Most readers today hear comfort. Your heart is a harsh judge, but it isn't the final one. God is greater: he knows everything, including what you've forgotten, the good you did and the reasons you struggled, and he is merciful. Some older commentators heard a warning instead: if even your own heart condemns you, how much more does God, who knows all things? Both readings take God's knowledge seriously. The first reading fits the paragraph's purpose, which is to settle the heart, and many churches lean on it. Then the writer goes on: "Beloved, if our heart condemn us not, then have we confidence toward God." Confidence is a word for freedom of speech, being able to speak openly, like a child who isn't afraid to ask. And he sums up the whole commandment in a single sentence: "That we should believe on the name of his Son Jesus Christ, and love one another." Believe and love. Two halves of one command. And then, for the first time in the letter, he names the way we know God lives in us: by the Spirit he has given us. Your heart is a narrator. It is not the judge.
screen: then, large: `GOD IS GREATER THAN OUR HEART.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: quiet your self-accusing. Settle, and breathe. Let the prosecutor speak for a moment. What is it saying today? Hear it out, without arguing. Then imagine something bigger than that voice standing beside you. Not to shout it down. To know more than it knows. The context it forgot. The good it skipped. The reasons it ignored. Breathe in, and let your shoulders drop. Breathe out, and let the voice get quieter. If you pray, you can bring the accusation to God and leave it there. The bell holds the time.
Greater than our heart. First John's word to the self-accusing: God knows all things, and is greater than the heart that condemns.
Your line: greater than your heart. Today, when the inner prosecutor starts up, say the line once in your head and then do the next good thing. Day six hundred eighty-seven.

688.title: Test the spirits (1 John 4:1–6)
688.hook: not every voice is from God; test it
688.howItsDone: Christians practice discernment by testing teachings against Scripture and the faith of the church, and many seek the help of a pastor, spiritual director or community; Ignatian discernment, from Ignatius of Loyola, is widely used.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the heart that condemns, and your line was greater than your heart. When the inner prosecutor started up, did you say the line? Day six hundred eighty-eight.

Before there were labs, people tested gold by rubbing it on a dark stone and looking at the streak it left. Real gold left one color. Fakes left another. The stone was called a touchstone, and it gave us the word. Jewelers still test metals today, with acids and scales. The point is the same: something can look exactly like gold and not be gold. First John has been all warmth and love for a while. Now, without warning, he says something brisk and practical: don't believe every voice. Test it.

In the King James Bible: "Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world." Try, here, is the Greek word for testing metal, the assayer's word. Notice he starts with beloved. This isn't a cynic talking. It's someone who loves his readers enough to want them not to be fooled. In his day, it seems, teachers were going around claiming the Spirit, and some of them said that Jesus didn't really come in a body. So the writer gives a test that fits his moment: "Every spirit that confesseth that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh is of God." Remember the opening of the letter: what our hands have handled. The test is whether a teaching holds on to a real, touchable Jesus. Then a word of courage: "greater is he that is in you, than he that is in the world." The reader isn't small and helpless before every persuasive voice. And then a sobering line: the world listens to its own. Popular doesn't mean true. Christians call this gift discernment. Paul lists the discerning of spirits among the Spirit's gifts. Over the centuries, churches have taught many ways to practice it. Catholic and Orthodox Christians often test a teaching against Scripture, the church's tradition and the guidance of the church. Many Protestants test it against Scripture first, and with the counsel of the community. Ignatius of Loyola wrote rules for discerning the spirits that many still use. All of them share the writer's starting point: some voices sound like gold. Test them before you trust them.
screen: `GREATER IS HE THAT IS IN YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: check one claim before believing it. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you heard or read this week that you accepted quickly. A headline, a rumor, a confident voice online, an inner voice that told you something about yourself. Hold it up like gold on a touchstone. Where did it come from? Who benefits if I believe it? Does it lead toward love, or away from it? Does it fit what I know to be true? Don't rush to a verdict. Just test it. If you pray, you can ask for discernment. The bell holds the time.
Discernment. The gift of testing voices before trusting them, the way a touchstone tells real gold from fake.
Your line: test the spirits. Today, before you share or repeat one thing, check where it came from. Day six hundred eighty-eight.

689.title: God is love (1 John 4:7–12)
689.hook: whoever loves is born of God, for God is love
689.howItsDone: 1 John 4:7–12 is one of the most often read passages at Christian weddings and funerals, and many churches use 'God is love' as a short summary of Christian faith when teaching children.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the word discernment, and your line was test the spirits. Which claim did you check before you shared it? Day six hundred eighty-nine.

Three words. You've seen them on church signs, wedding programs, bumper stickers, tattoos, and embroidered on pillows in a grandmother's living room. They've been printed so often they can start to sound like wallpaper. But they come from one place, this letter, and they were not written as decoration. The writer has just told his readers to test every spirit, to watch out for voices that sound right and aren't. And then, right after that warning, he says the truest thing he knows. Today we hear those three words where they actually live.

In the King James Bible: "Beloved, let us love one another: for love is of God; and every one that loveth is born of God, and knoweth God." Love comes from God, the way light comes from the sun. Then the reverse: "He that loveth not knoweth not God; for God is love." Notice the order of those words. God is love. Not love is God. In the Greek the grammar makes that clear: God is the subject. The writer isn't saying that whatever we feel as love is divine. He's saying that the deepest truth about God is love. So how do we know what that love looks like? He doesn't leave it abstract. "Herein is love, not that we loved God, but that he loved us, and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins." The love starts on God's side, not ours. Propitiation is a heavy word; it means the offering that makes things right between us and God. Christians explain how that works in different ways, but they agree on the direction: love reaching first. Then a startling line: "No man hath seen God at any time." Nobody. And yet, the next words: "If we love one another, God dwelleth in us, and his love is perfected in us." The invisible God becomes visible, in a sense, wherever people love. Four centuries later, Augustine preached a series of sermons on this letter. In one of them he said, in Latin, dilige, et quod vis fac: love, and do what you will. He didn't mean anything goes. He meant that if love is truly the root, what grows from it will be good.
screen: `GOD IS LOVE, NOT LOVE IS GOD.`
`HE LOVED US FIRST, AND SENT HIS SON.`
`NO ONE HAS SEEN GOD. LOVE SHOWS HIM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: love someone without conditions, starting here. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone you love, but with a few conditions attached. If they'd only call more. If they'd stop that habit. If they'd say sorry first. Picture their face. Then, gently, set the conditions down, one at a time, as if you were taking stones out of your pockets. What's left when they're gone? Stay with that. Notice how it feels to love them as they are, this minute. If you pray, you can pray for them, and give thanks that love reached you first. The bell holds the time.
God is love. Three words from First John: love starts on God's side, and wherever people love one another, the unseen God dwells.
Your line: god is love. Today, with the person you pictured, drop one condition for one whole day, and see what changes. Day six hundred eighty-nine.

690.title: Perfect love casts out fear (1 John 4:13–18)
690.hook: there is no fear in love
690.howItsDone: Many Christians memorize 1 John 4:18 and pray it in times of anxiety, and pastors often use it to distinguish reverent awe of God from dread of punishment.

segments.voice: Yesterday, three words, and your line was god is love. Which condition did you set down for a day? Day six hundred ninety.

Watch a toddler at the playground. They run off, climb something too high, look around, and find their parent's face. If the face is there, they go a little farther. If it isn't, panic. Psychologists have a name for this, a secure base: a child who's sure of being loved explores more, not less. Fear shrinks the world; love widens it. The writer of First John never read a psychology textbook. But he says something very close, in a single short verse about what love does to fear.

First he repeats yesterday's great line and adds to it. In the King James Bible: "God is love; and he that dwelleth in love dwelleth in God, and God in him." Dwelleth means to live in, to stay, to make your home in. Love isn't only something God does; it's a place you can live. Then the verse: "There is no fear in love; but perfect love casteth out fear: because fear hath torment. He that feareth is not made perfect in love." Three things to notice. First, perfect doesn't mean flawless. The Greek word means complete, full-grown, mature. Grown-up love, not spotless love. Second, casteth out is a strong verb. It's the word for throwing something out the door. Love doesn't negotiate with fear. It shows it out. Third, fear hath torment. The word for torment can also mean punishment. The kind of fear he means is the dread of being punished, the fear of a child who expects to be hit. Here a fair question comes up. Doesn't the Bible also talk about the fear of the Lord? It does, often. Many Christian teachers have distinguished two kinds of fear. One is reverence, awe before something holy, like standing at the edge of the ocean. The other is dread, cringing before a punisher. The writer seems to mean the second. Reverence can stay. Dread is what love throws out. And the letter's context is judgment day: he says we can have boldness even then. Not because we're flawless, but because, as he says, as he is, so are we in this world.
screen: then, large: `THERE IS NO FEAR IN LOVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let love answer one fear. Settle, and breathe. Name one fear that has been with you lately. Being found out. Being left. Getting it wrong. Getting sick. Say it plainly in your mind. Now ask it one question: what are you afraid will happen to me? Listen. Then, beside it, picture the face of someone who loves you, or, if you pray, the love of God. Don't argue with the fear. Just let love stand in the same room with it. Notice which one takes up more space after a minute. The bell holds the time.
Perfect love casts out fear. Full-grown love throws out the dread of punishment, so that people can live without torment, even before God.
screen: `PERFECT LOVE CASTS OUT FEAR — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: no fear in love. Today, do one thing you've been avoiding out of fear, a call, a question, a no, and do it from love instead. Day six hundred ninety.

691.title: We love because (1 John 4:19–21)
691.hook: we love him because he first loved us
691.howItsDone: Many Christians memorize 1 John 4:19 as a short summary of their faith, and churches often teach it to children; it is also a common verse at baptisms and weddings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, perfect love casts out fear, and your line was no fear in love. What did you do from love that fear had been holding back? Day six hundred ninety-one.

Nobody teaches a baby to smile back. A parent leans over the crib, smiles, makes a silly noise, and smiles again. For weeks, nothing. Then one morning, the baby smiles back. The first smile isn't the baby's idea. It's an answer. It was learned by being smiled at. Today's passage is only three verses long, one of the shortest of our readings in First John. And its first line is about exactly that: which love comes first, and which one answers.

In the King James Bible: "We love him, because he first loved us." Simple, short, and it holds the whole letter. Our love is a response. God's love goes first. And here's a detail worth knowing. Some of the oldest Greek manuscripts don't have the word him. They read simply: we love, because he first loved us. Read that way, it isn't only, we love God because God loved us. It's, we love at all, anyone at all, because we were loved first. The source of every kind of love, for God and for neighbor, is the same. Then the writer makes it very concrete, and very uncomfortable: "If a man say, I love God, and hateth his brother, he is a liar: for he that loveth not his brother whom he hath seen, how can he love God whom he hath not seen?" He's not being harsh for the fun of it. He's pointing out something simple. God is invisible. Your brother is right in front of you, with all his irritating habits. If you can't love the one you can see, the claim to love the one you can't is hard to believe. It's a test anyone can apply to themselves, and nobody passes it perfectly. That's why it matters that the love started on the other side. And then the last line of this section: "And this commandment have we from him, That he who loveth God love his brother also." Not two commandments, one for God and one for people. One. Love God, and the love spills sideways. The letter has been circling this for four chapters. Light, children, deeds, fear. Here it lands: we love, because he first loved us.
screen: then, large: `BECAUSE HE FIRST LOVED US.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: receive love before giving it. Settle, and breathe. Don't try to love anyone for a minute. Instead, remember being loved. A parent's voice. A friend who stayed. A teacher who believed you could. A stranger's kindness on a bad day. Let one memory come, and stay in it. Let yourself be on the receiving end, without hurrying to pay it back. Notice where you feel it in your body. If you pray, you can receive God's love the same way, with nothing to do but be loved. Then, only at the end, notice whether you feel like smiling back. The bell holds the time.
We love because. The heart of First John: all our love is an answer, because he first loved us.
Your line: he first loved us. Today, thank one person who loved you first, before you'd done anything to earn it. Day six hundred ninety-one.

692.title: That you may know (1 John 5)
692.hook: the letter ends: little children, keep yourselves from idols
692.howItsDone: Many Christians read 1 John 5:13 as a word of assurance, and in teaching and preaching the letter's last line about idols is often applied to anything, not only statues, that takes God's place in a life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, we love because, and your line was he first loved us. Did you let yourself receive some love before you gave any? Day six hundred ninety-two.

Some letters bury the point in the middle. This one saves it for the end. First John is a long, circling letter: light and darkness, love and fear, little children, test the spirits. Then, in the last chapter, the writer gives what many readers take as his reason for writing all of it. And he signs off with a line that seems to come out of nowhere. Not grace be with you. Not peace. Just this: little children, keep yourselves from idols. No explanation, and then amen. Today, the last chapter of First John: the reason for the whole letter, and its strange parting shot.

The chapter opens with how love works in practice. In the King James Bible: "For this is the love of God, that we keep his commandments: and his commandments are not grievous." Not grievous: not heavy, not a crushing load. And then: "this is the victory that overcometh the world, even our faith." Then comes the purpose of the whole letter, in verse thirteen: "These things have I written unto you that believe on the name of the Son of God; that ye may know that ye have eternal life." That ye may know. Not hope, not guess, not lie awake wondering at 2am. Many readers hear the Greek verb here as settled knowing, the kind you don't have to keep checking. The letter has spent five chapters on tests: do you walk in the light, do you love your brother. You might think the point was to make readers anxious. The writer says the opposite. He wrote so they could stop wondering and rest. One small history note. If you read verse seven in the King James Bible, you'll find a line about three that bear record in heaven: the Father, the Word and the Holy Ghost. That line isn't in the early Greek manuscripts. It came in through the Latin tradition, and most modern translations leave it out or put it in a footnote. Churches that teach the Trinity draw it from many passages and the early creeds, not from this one verse. And then the ending: "Little children, keep yourselves from idols." Scholars aren't sure what he had in mind. Maybe the temple statues in a city like Ephesus, where tradition places the elder. Maybe the false pictures of God the letter has been warning about. Maybe anything that quietly takes God's place. The letter doesn't say. It just leaves the line ringing, like a parent calling after you at the door: take care of yourselves.
screen: `WRITTEN SO YOU CAN KNOW, NOT GUESS.`
`A VERSE THE EARLY GREEK DOESN'T HAVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name one idol, gently. Settle, and breathe. In the old sense, an idol is something carved and bowed to. In the wider sense many Christians use, it's anything sitting in the center where something truer belongs. Your phone, maybe. Someone's approval. Money, a grudge, a plan for how life has to go. Let one come to mind. Don't scold it. Just name it, quietly, the way you'd name a houseguest who has stayed too long. Then let each breath move it one inch from the center. If you pray, you can rest on the old line from Psalm 46: be still, and know that I am God. The bell holds the time.
That you may know. The reason First John gives for itself: so its readers could stop guessing, and know they have life.
Your line: that you may know. Today, when a doubt or a worry shows up, notice it, and then go back to one thing you already know is true. Day six hundred ninety-two.

693.title: Face to face (2 and 3 John)
693.hook: two postcards from the elder: I'd rather not write with ink, but talk face to face
693.howItsDone: Many Christian communities treat hospitality and visiting, especially of the sick, the homebound and travelers, as part of their life together, and 3 John's praise of Gaius is often read as a picture of that welcome.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the end of First John, and your line was that you may know. What idol did you name, gently? Day six hundred ninety-three.

Count the times this week you texted someone you could have called, or called someone you could have visited. No judgment. Everyone does it. Two thousand years ago, a church leader who calls himself simply the elder felt the pull the other way. Two of his notes survive in the Bible, Second and Third John, among the shortest books in it, each small enough to fit on a single sheet of papyrus. And both end with almost the same line: I have more to say, but I'd rather not say it in ink. I'd rather come and talk to you face to face.
screen: `I'D RATHER NOT WRITE IT IN INK.`

segments.voice: Second John is addressed "unto the elect lady and her children, whom I love in the truth." Nobody knows who she is. She might be a woman who hosted a church in her home. Many scholars think the elect lady is a way of naming a whole congregation, with her children as its members. The note repeats the heart of First John: love one another, walk in his commandments, and be careful of teachers who deny that Jesus came in the flesh. Third John is a note to one man, "the wellbeloved Gaius," and it reads like a personal letter. There's praise for Gaius, who opened his home to traveling teachers. There's a complaint about a man named Diotrephes, "who loveth to have the preeminence among them," and who turned those same travelers away. And there's a good word for someone called Demetrius. Church drama, two thousand years old, in a few lines. Then both notes end the same way. In the King James Bible, Second John says: "Having many things to write unto you, I would not write with paper and ink: but I trust to come unto you, and speak face to face, that our joy may be full." Here's the surprise: the Greek doesn't actually say face to face. It says mouth to mouth, stoma pros stoma. Speak with your own mouth, close enough to hear the voice. The elder knew what ink can't carry: a tone, a hand on the shoulder, the look on someone's face when they finally understand. And that closes this week. Greater than your heart. Test the spirits. God is love. No fear in love. He first loved us. That you may know. And now, face to face. A whole week about love, ending with an elder who would rather show up in person than write it down.
screen: `THE ELECT LADY: A WOMAN, OR A CHURCH?`
`A WEEK OF LOVE, ENDING IN PERSON.`
then, large: `THAT OUR JOY MAY BE FULL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: visit someone instead of messaging. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone you mostly know through a screen these days: a grandparent, an old friend, a neighbor you only wave at. Picture their face. Not their profile picture: their actual face, the way it moves when they laugh. Then, in the quiet, choose one small way to be in the same room soon. A coffee, a walk, a knock on the door. If a visit isn't possible, a call where they can hear your voice counts. If you pray, you can hold their name for a moment. The bell holds the time.
